cands.bio: Democrat representing California's 43rd District since 2013. She served in the U.S. House from 1991 (previously the 29th and 35th Districts) and in the California Assembly from 1977 to 1991. She chaired the House Financial Services Committee 2019–2023 and is now its ranking member. Earlier she worked as a Head Start assistant teacher and as chief deputy to a Los Angeles city councilman.

controversies.text: Missed 30 of 676 U.S. House votes this Congress (4.4%), counted from the roll calls through 2026-09-16. Longest run of misses: 5, 2025-12-18 to 2025-12-18.

The House Ethics Committee examined whether Waters improperly helped OneUnited Bank, where her husband held stock. On September 21, 2012, it voted 10-0 that the evidence did not establish a violation by her. It found her chief of staff acted for the bank despite her instructions to avoid the conflict, and reproved him.

On April 17, 2021, at a Minnesota protest, Waters said that if Derek Chauvin weren't convicted, protesters should "get more confrontational." The trial judge denied a mistrial but called officials' failure to respect the court "abhorrent." A censure resolution failed. Waters said she meant confronting the justice system and nonviolent action.

endorsements.text: 2026 endorsements listed by Ballotpedia include the Democratic Party of California, the California Federation of Labor Unions (AFL-CIO), the National Union of Healthcare Workers, Equality California, California Environmental Voters, and the Sierra Club Angeles Chapter.

cands.gaps: We found no documented positions or actions by Waters on data centers, homestead property taxes, limits on investor or foreign land buyers, growth and land protection, police pay and pensions, gun laws, or school choice and teacher pay. She did not complete Ballotpedia's 2024 or 2026 candidate surveys, so there are no self-reported platform statements. The Ballotpedia page was cut off partway through its 117th Congress section, so earlier-session details were not read. Her Wikipedia biography was also cut off before its later political-positions sections, and no photo or source was found for her upbringing beyond high school in St. Louis.

cands.name: Cristian Morales

money.note: Individuals gave $2,250; PAC money $0; candidate's own money $0. Percentages describe itemized individual gifts, which the FEC has processed through about July 2026.

cands.bio: Republican candidate for U.S. House in California's 43rd District in 2026. Born in Guatemala City. Business executive and director of operations with a 20+ year manufacturing career in automotive, aerospace and defense. Ran for governor in 2022 and lost the primary. Has held no elected office.

endorsements.text: Republican Party of California, listed by Ballotpedia among his 2026 endorsements. His own survey also lists the Los Angeles Republican Party, California Republican Assembly, Reform California and Restoring The California Dream.

cands.gaps: We could not find when Morales moved to California or how long he has lived in the state. The sources do not name his employers or the dates of his jobs. He has held no office, so there is no record of official actions. We found no stated positions from him on data centers, homestead property taxes, limits on investor or foreign land buying, growth and land protection, foreign or big-donor money, abortion, or red-flag laws. He has not stated a position on H-1B visas or E-Verify. He says his nonprofit runs a Northern Triangle and Triark Project, but we found nothing describing it. No news coverage or controversies were found.

second-amendment.evidence: Said on his 2022 campaign website, "I am a staunch supporter of gun rights," and argued that gun-control restrictions would be undercut by cartel-supplied weapons.

school-choice-teachers.evidence: Said on his 2022 campaign website, "I am a firm supporter of school choice," while also calling himself an advocate for teachers' unions. He did not state a teacher pay figure.

back-police-order.evidence: Said on his 2022 campaign website that he "won't tolerate violent crime," criticized district attorneys in San Francisco and Los Angeles for reducing crime penalties, and in his 2022 survey backed a "3 strikes and you are out" rule for violent crime.
